summary: Specifies a Telnet option for hosts that want to support the 3270 data stream inside Telnet. It was a proposed standard, and is now historic. It was updated by RFC 6270.

plainLanguage.summary: Some old mainframe terminals have their own special screen language. This option lets them be used through a Telnet connection, a general remote-login link.

questions: what is the telnet 3270 regime option
how to use 3270 terminals over telnet
subtitle: A Telnet option that lets a client and server agree on a 3270 terminal type in one negotiation.

tldr.problem: Using the IBM 3270 data stream over Telnet required three separate options (TERMINALTYPE, BINARY and EOR) with no specified order, and no standard way to leave 3270 mode.
tldr.mechanism: The 3270-REGIME option (code 29) has the client send a list of terminal types it supports and the server reply with one, which implies binary data and an EOR delimiter.
tldr.outcome: It was proposed as a standard in 1988. The unit metadata lists it as Historic and updated by RFC 6270.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 1041 as Historic and updated by RFC 6270. The text itself was a proposed standard from January 1988.

sections.title: Why a 3270 Regime Option
sections.content:
RFC 1041 lets a Telnet server on VM or MVS negotiate with a Telnet client whether to use the 3270 data stream or plain NVT ASCII. Before it, 3270 support needed three options negotiated together: TERMINALTYPE, BINARY and EOR. The order was never specified, it was unclear when 3270 mode was actually in effect, TERMINALTYPE could offer only one terminal type at a time, and there was no standard way back to NVT ASCII.

Establishing the 3270 regime now implies three things: every character is 8 bits of binary data, both sides use IAC EOR as a delimiter, and both sides agree on a terminal type. The memo does not define the 3270 protocols themselves, and treats colors, graphics and keyboard mapping as outside Telnet or a local matter. Features such as color may be negotiated indirectly through terminal type names.
sections.plainLanguage: Before this, the two computers had to have three separate chats to set up a mainframe terminal, and nobody said in what order. Now it is one chat.

sections.title: Commands and Subnegotiation
sections.content:
The option is named 3270-REGIME with code 29. WILL and DO grant permission for a later subnegotiation, and WON'T and DON'T refuse it. The default is WON'T/DON'T, meaning no 3270 regime.

Two subnegotiations carry the content. IAC SB 3270-REGIME ARE REGIME-LIST IAC SE (code 1) lists every regime the sender supports. IAC SB 3270-REGIME IS REGIME IAC SE (code 0) states the one chosen, which must be a substring of the received list. The list is an ASCII string of terminal type names separated by spaces, with embedded spaces and backslashes escaped by a backslash. An empty list or empty regime means NVT ASCII only.
sections.plainLanguage: The terminal hands over a menu of the kinds it can be, and the computer circles one.

sections.title: How the Negotiation Runs
sections.content:
Either side may start the option, but both must exchange WILL 3270-REGIME and DO 3270-REGIME before subnegotiation. To keep it simple, only the client may send ARE and only the server may reply with IS. Because it is asymmetric, each renegotiation repeats the whole process.

The RFC's example has the client send ibm3279-3 ibm3279-2 ibm3278-3, and the server answer ibm3279-2. Lists run from most to least desirable, and the receiver picks the first type it supports. Sending an empty list switches both sides to NVT ASCII. To change terminal type without accidentally dropping to NVT ASCII, include both the current and new types in the list.
sections.plainLanguage: The terminal lists its favorites first, and the computer takes the first one it knows how to handle.

sections.title: Implementation Rules
sections.content:
Because IAC (255 decimal) is used as a delimiter with EOR, an IAC that is part of the data must be escaped with another IAC. To avoid ambiguity during negotiation, the client should accept no user data once negotiation starts and send nothing after ARE. The server should try not to send data meanwhile, and may reply with IS only after all outstanding data has been sent.

The server switches regimes only after sending IS, and the client only after receiving it. A switch may require flushing outstanding data on both sides.
sections.plainLanguage: While they are deciding, both sides stop talking about anything else, so nothing gets mixed up.
